abstract: The complement system, a key innate immunity component, is implicated in COVID-19 pathogenesis. Proteomic studies reveal dysregulated complement and coagulation cascades (CCC) proteins in COVID-19, yet comprehensive analyses remain limited. This bioinformatics study analyzed proteomic data (from inception to January 13, 2025) across Web of Science, PubMed, EMBASE, and Wiley Online Library using keywords “complement and coagulation cascades”, “COVID-19”, and “proteomics”. Included studies compared differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) in COVID-19 patients versus healthy controls. Two reviewers independently extracted data. DEPs were analyzed via R (v4.4.2), Stata (v14), and STRING (v12.0). Twenty studies identified 3,018 DEPs, including 58 CCC-related genes (e.g., FGB , SERPINA5 , FGG , F2 ). Hub genes were identified using MCODE and cytohubba in Cytoscape, and 16 hub genes (e.g., FGB , SERPINA5 ) were found. Stata confirmed consistent expression of FGB , SERPINA5 , FGG , and F2 . All of them are the biomarkers of diseases, and are the drug targets except SERPINA5 according to the reports from OpenTargets database. Immunohistochemistry validated FGB upregulation and SERPINA5 downregulation. In summary, CCC pathway proteins are extensively dysregulated in COVID-19. FGB and SERPINA5 are potential diagnostic biomarkers and therapeutic targets, offering insights into severe COVID-19 mechanisms and guiding novel treatment strategies. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12879-025-11598-8.

Materials and methods
Search strategy
This study adhered to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews (PRISMA) guidelines [
7
]. A comprehensive search was conducted across four databases—PUBMED, Web of Science (WOS), EMBASE, and WILEY Online Library—using the keywords of ‘complement and coagulation cascades’, ‘COVID-19’, and ‘proteomics’. In PUBMED, these terms were searched across all fields. In WOS, they were restricted to titles, abstracts, and indexing. For EMBASE, filters included full text, human studies, COVID-19, English language, and exclusion of preprint records. In WILEY Online Library, only full articles were exported to EndNote, excluding abstracts, guidelines, supplements, oral sessions, posters, issue information, talks, and books. References from relevant studies were also screened. Initial screening of the title and abstracts of all papers was performed independently by two authors (Siyuan Liu, Huichun Shi). Based on relevance criteria, they selected full-text articles for detailed evaluation. Final inclusion decisions were made by consensus between the two reviewers. Any disagreements arising during this phase were resolved through adjudication by a third reviewer (Lijun ZHANG). The study selection process, following PRISMA 2020, was summarized in Fig.
1
.
Fig. 1
Flow chart of the selection process of the studies included in this systematic review of complement and coagulation cascades pathway in COVID-19, following PRISMA 2020. MS, mass spectrometry
Eligibility criteria
The inclusion criteria for articles were as follows: (a) studies involving proteome profiling and quantification using mass spectrometry; (b) research conducted on adult human samples; (c) comparisons between COVID-19 patients and healthy controls; and (d) primary data clearly presenting differential groups, with DEPs that could be extracted or recalculated.
Studies focusing solely on the effects of specific treatments in COVID-19 patients or only having samples from the treated patients were excluded. Additionally, conference abstracts, case reports, case series, letters, editorials, guidelines, theses, commentaries, reviews, systematic reviews, brief communications, and technical notes were not considered. Articles retrieved from the search were managed using Endnote (version 21).
Data extraction and risk of bias assessment
DEPs were
identified
using the following thresholds: a fold change of ≤ 0.667 or ≥ 1.500 and a
p
-value < 0.05. For DEPs identified in differential expression comparisons from references 16 and 20, only those common to all comparisons were extracted and their average fold changes were used for functional enrichment analysis. For meta-analysis, the data from each comparison were used. Two reviewers independently extracted data in accordance with PRISMA guidelines, resolving discrepancies through discussion. Data management and analysis were performed using R Studio (version 4.4.2).
Functional enrichment analysis
Genes associated with the CCC pathway were retrieved from the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) database (
http://www.genome.jp/kegg/genes.html
) and matched with DEPs using R software. The matched DEPs within the CCC pathway were analyzed using STRING software (version 12.0), with a confidence threshold set at a Kappa score of 0.7 and a false discovery rate (FDR) below 0.05. A protein-protein interaction (PPI) network was constructed using Cytoscape v3.10.0-BETA1 software [
8
], with the matched CCC pathway genes serving as nodes.
The Molecular Complex Detection (MCODE) plugin [
9
] was used to identify submodules within the PPI network generated by Cytoscape. Parameters included a degree cutoff of 2, node score cutoff of 0.2, k-core of 2, max depth of 100, and a minimum of 4 genes per module. Hub genes were identified using the cytoHubba plugin [
10
], employing ranked nodes and the maximal clique centrality (MCC) algorithm.
Meta-Analysis
Hub genes reported in at least two studies were included and analyzed by the randomeffects metaanalysis using Stata 14.0 (Stata Software, USA). Log2 Fold Change (Log2 FC) and negative Log
P
-value (-Log
P
) were extracted from each study, with Log2 FC indicating difference between the COVID-19 and healthy controls, and –Log
P
reflecting statistical significance. The weighted average method was applied to compute the meta-analysis effect size, where Log2 FC values were weighted by their corresponding –Log
P
to prioritize studies with higher statistical significance.
The 95% confidence intervals (CIs) of the combined estimates were derived based on these weights. Forest plots were generated to visualize the expression trends and statistical robustness of each gene across studies. Between-study heterogeneity was assessed using the
I
² statistic, and a pooled estimate was considered statistically significant if its 95% CI did not include zero (0).
Potential drug target analyses
To identify promising therapeutic candidates, we evaluated the druggability of nine hub genes utilizing the Open Targets Platform
[
11
]
. Disease associations and existing pharmacological compounds were subsequently examined.
Immunohistochemical validation of FGB and SERPINA5 expression
The experimental procedures were approved by ethics committee of Shanghai Public Health Clinical Center (Protocol No. 2023-S077-01, approved on July 4, 2023). Six patients with COVID-19, and seven patients with lung cancer were involved (Supplement Table
1
(Table
S1
)). Lung tissue specimens from both COVID-19 patients and healthy controls (adjacent normal tissues from the patients with lung cancer) were processed for immunohistochemical analysis. Tissue sections were treated with specific primary antibodies: fibrinogen beta chain [
EPR19765
] (ab193932, ABcam, Cambridge, UK) (1:400 dilutions) and Serpin A5 [EPR23337-112] (ab270451) (1:400 dilutions). Subsequent staining and imaging procedures were performed using the automated BOND RX Research Stainer (Leica Biosystems, Illinois, United States). Then we performed semi-quantitative assessment of
FGB
and
SERPINA5
expression levels in pulmonary specimens through counting positive cells, ten random microscopic fields were captured per section at 400× magnification. Quantitative analysis involved enumerating immunoreactive cells within each field. Protein expression alterations were determined by calculating the ratio between mean positive cell counts from 60 microscopic fields (6 COVID-19 cases) and 70 fields (7 control cases).
Furthermore, we also quantified the expression of
FGB
and
SERPINA5
using optical density measurement. Slide imaging was performed with the TissueFAXS 200 system (TissueFAXS Viewer software, Tissue Gnostics, Vienna, Austria), followed by quantitative analysis using HistoQuest software (version 6.0.1.114). Through systematic parameter optimization, we enhanced three critical analytical components: total slide area demarcation, positive cell identification, and background signal subtraction. Gene expression levels were calculated as the mean intensity of positive cells.

Introduction
Since its emergence in December 2019, COVID-19 has become a global pandemic, impacting millions of individuals worldwide. Although the epidemic has been subsided, it remains a public health challenge due to the continuous evolution of SARS-CoV-2 and its persistence in certain regions [
1
]. Many individuals continue to experience “long COVID”, which affects multiple systems, including the respiratory, gastrointestinal, musculoskeletal, nervous, and endocrine systems [
2
]. Understanding the mechanisms and finding new biomarkers of SARS-CoV-2 infection remains crucial.
In our prior proteomic analysis of lung tissues from COVID-19 patients, we observed dysregulation of proteins in the complement and coagulation cascades (CCC) pathway compared to adjacent tissues [
3
]. During infection, the cytokine storm triggers excessive inflammation, complement-mediated endothelial damage, and widespread microvascular thrombosis [
4
,
5
]. Proteins in CCC pathway are involved in these activities [
6
]. To systematically investigate these proteins, we reviewed proteomic studies on COVID-19 patients, identifying differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) associated with the CCC pathway. These DEPs were extracted from existing literature, integrated, and analyzed using bioinformatics tools. Two key hub genes,
FGB
(fibrinogen beta chain) and
SERPINA5
(plasma serine protease inhibitor, serpin A5), were further validated through immunohistochemistry. This study aims to enhance the understanding of the molecular mechanisms of COVID-19 and explore potential biomarkers and therapeutic strategies.

Based on relevance criteria, they selected full-text articles for detailed evaluation. Final inclusion decisions were made by consensus between the two reviewers. Any disagreements arising during this phase were resolved through adjudication by a third reviewer (Lijun ZHANG). The study selection process, following PRISMA 2020, was summarized in Fig.

A total of 3,018 DEPs meeting the threshold of 1.5-fold change (
p
< 0.05) were initially identified. Proteins that did not have a matching gene name were summarized based on their Uniprot ID. The final dataset comprised 2,352 unique genes for subsequent analysis.
Genes in the CCC pathway
Through comparative analysis of 20 publications against the CCC pathway’s 88-gene repertoire, we identified 58 overlapping genetic markers with detailed expressions presented in Table S2. Of these 58 genes, 30 were detected in at least two articles, including eight demonstrating conserved upregulation, five showing consistent downregulation, and 17 exhibiting discordant regulatory patterns across different investigations. These 58 genes exhibited broad representation across all five complement pathways (extrinsic, intrinsic, classical, lectin and alternative pathway) (Figure S1). Furthermore, we also analyzed these 58 genes using STRING database, and found that the most significantly enriched KEGG pathway was the CCC pathway, followed by
Staphylococcus aureus
infection, pertussis, and systemic lupus erythematosus (Fig. 2 A). Protein-protein interaction analysis revealed strong connectivity between these genes (Fig.
2
B).

Nine hub gene expression revealed by meta-analysis
Hub genes identified in ≥ 2 independent studies (Table
2
) underwent systematic meta-analysis. Figure
3
A demonstrates that four consensus hub genes (
F2
,
SERPINA5
,
FGB
, and
FGG
) maintained statistically significant differential expression (
p
< 0.05) between COVID-19 patients and healthy controls across heterogeneous cohorts. Specifically, the Log₂ FC values for
F2
and
SERPINA5
were − 1.59 (95% CI: −2.09, −1.09) and − 1.11 (95% CI: −1.27, −0.94), respectively, indicating downregulation. In contrast,
FGB
and
FGG
were upregulated, with Log₂ FC values of 1.31 (95% CI: 0.86, 1.77) and 1.38 (95% CI: 0.93, 1.82), respectively. Notably, the absence of between-study heterogeneity (
I
² = 0.0%) observed for
F2
and
SERPINA5
demonstrates absolute consistency in differential expression patterns across all analyzed cohorts.

Among the five genes with inconsistent expression patterns (
FGA
,

FGA

showed downregulation with a Log₂ FC of −0.51 (95% CI: −0.92, −0.10). Although the combined effects for these two genes are statistically significant, their high

² values of 88.4% and 93.7% indicate substantial heterogeneity across studies. The heterogeneity for these gene expression may be largely influenced by factors such as study design, sample type, sample size, or data analysis methods. Therefore, despite statistical significance, the biological reproducibility of these findings should be interpreted with caution. In the further, it is necessary to verify these expressions by different methods.
Evaluating the druggability profile of four central hub genes
Leveraging the Open Targets database, we systematically assessed the disease associations of the four different hub genes (
F2
,
FGB
,
FGG
, and
SERPINA5
) (Table
2
). All genes were related to diseases. For example,
FGB
and
FGG
exhibited strong links to coagulation disorders, including congenital afibrinogenemia, familial afibrinogenemia, and familial dysfibrinogenemia. Similarly,
F2
was implicated in congenital prothrombin deficiency, factor II deficiency, and thrombophilia via thrombin dysfunction. While,
SERPINA5
demonstrated associations with quantitative blood protein measurements (e.g., sex hormone-binding globulin and serum albumin levels). For targeted drug analysis, FDA-approved anticoagulants (fibrinogen/plasminogen-based therapies) targeted
FGB
/
FGG
, and direct thrombin inhibitors (lepirudin, dabigatran, bivalirudin) targeted
F2
. However, no clinically approved drugs currently target
SERPINA5
, highlighting its unexplored therapeutic potential (Table
2
).
FGB and SERPINA5 were verified by immunohistochemical analysis
Despite prior reports of dysregulated
FGB
(upregulated in six studies) and
SERPINA5
(downregulated in four studies) in COVID-19, empirical validation through gold-standard protein detection methods (e.g., IHC, western blot, ELISA) remained absent. To address this methodological gap, we performed IHC validation in COVID-19 lung tissues versus healthy controls. Anti-Fibrinogen beta chain staining revealed pronounced
FGB
accumulation in patient tissues (Fig.
4
A) compared to that in the controls (Fig.
4
B). Conversely,
SERPINA5
exhibited marked depletion in COVID-19 samples (Fig. 4 C) relative to the levels in healthy lungs (Fig.
4
D). Quantitative histomorphometric assessment at 400× magnification confirmed the differential expression profiles:
FGB
-positive cells exhibited a 1.5-fold elevation in COVID-19 patients (161 ± 97 vs. 107 ± 40 in controls;
p
< 0.0001, Fig.
4
E), whereas
SERPINA5
immunoreactivity displayed a 1.3-fold decrease (111 ± 45 vs.144 ± 63
p
< 0.01, Fig. 4 F). Furthermore, we also quantified
FGB
and
SERPINA5
by optical density method, and found that
FGB
was upregulated for 1.4-fold (Fig.
4
G, while
SEPRINA5
decreased for 1.9-fold (Fig.
4
H). These orthogonal validation bridges proteomic predictions with histopathological evidence, resolving prior discrepancies in experimental confirmation.

Discussion
Despite successful containment of the COVID-19 pandemic via global vaccine deployment and natural immunity acquisition, the virus remains a persistent source of severe morbidity, with age- and comorbidity-dependent progression to fatal outcomes. Current epidemiological data reveal 12–15% of hospitalized patients develop life-threatening complications, while 30% of survivors exhibit post-acute syndrome beyond six months. These unresolved clinical trajectories necessitate: (1) systems-level elucidation of viral-host interaction networks, and (2) discovery of stage-specific biomarkers to guide precision management strategies.
The complement system serves as a cornerstone of innate immunity, with its dysregulation emerging as a key mechanistic link in COVID-19 progression from mild to severe phenotypes [
33
]. Clinical evidence supports complement-targeted interventions, including C1 esterase inhibitors [
34
], and compstatin-based C3 inhibitors [
35
], demonstrating therapeutic efficacy in severe cases. This pathophysiological axis is further reinforced by multi-omics studies identifying extensive COVID-19-associated perturbations in CCC proteins [
3
,
14
,
18
,
22
]. Building on our prior discovery of eight upregulated CCC components (
FGA
,
FGB
,
FGG
,
ITGB2
,
ITGAM
,
ITGAX
,
PLAUR
, and
VSIG4
) in COVID-19 lung tissue [
3
], we conducted a systematic review of 20 proteomic studies, revealing dysregulation in 65.9% (58/88) of CCC pathway genes. Notably, all five complement activation routes (classical, lectin, alternative, intrinsic, and extrinsic pathways) exhibited significant protein-level disturbances, suggesting complement system involvement in SARS-CoV-2 pathogenesis. These findings demonstrate pan-regulatory dysregulation of the complement-coagulation axis in COVID-19 pathogenesis, suggesting that precision targeting of these molecular nodes (e.g., with monoclonal antibodies or small-molecule inhibitors) could rebuilding immune-thrombotic homeostasis in critically ill patients.
To discover the key regulators in the CCC pathway, we performed an integrative bioinformatics analysis using cytoscape with MCODE and cytoHubba plugins, and identified 16 high-confidence hub genes across two functionally distinct modules (MCODE1 and MCODE2). Cross-platform validation revealed four consistently dysregulated hub genes—
FGB
,
FGG
,
F2
, and
SERPINA5
, which exhibited conserved differential expression patterns in COVID-19 pathogenesis compared with the healthy. Of them,
FGB
and
FGG
are upregulated in COVID-19. Proteolytic processing of
FGB
by thrombin generates fibrin monomers that undergo structural co-polymerization with
FGA
/
FGG
subunits, forming cross-linked fibrin matrices essential for hemostatic plug formation.
FGB
upregulation might contribute to COVID-19–related pulmonary fibrosis through crosstalk with the TGF-β signaling pathway [
36
]. As a key fibrin precursor, elevated
FGB
can enhance TGF-β-induced myofibroblast activation and recruitment, leading to excessive extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition and tissue remodeling [
37
]. TGF-β1 not only directly promotes the expression of profibrotic genes, such as collagen and fibronectin, but also indirectly exacerbates pathology by inducing endothelial cell apoptosis and driving glomerular and interstitial fibrosis [
38
]. Consequently, increased
FGB
expression may aggravate lung injury and fibrosis in severe COVID-19 cases. A previous study showed that all variants of SARS-CoV-2 infections exhibited the capacity to provoke fibrin deposition in human lung epithelial cells [
39
]. Another two hub genes were
F2
and
SERPINA5
that were downregulated in COVID-19. Studies indicate reducing
F2
to 10% of normal levels resulted in 100% mortality in the mice infected with lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus clone 13 [
40
].
SERPINA5
downregulation may weaken host antiviral defense. This serine protease inhibitor regulates coagulation, inflammation, and host-pathogen interactions [
41
]; its reduced expression could result in uncontrolled protease activity, impaired epithelial barrier integrity, and enhanced viral replication. Previous studies indicate that
SERPINA5
contributes to antibacterial defense and resistance to HIV-1 infection, suggesting a potential protective role against SARS-CoV-2 [
42
]. Therefore, we hypothesized that these four hub genes (
FGG
,
FGB
,
F2
, and
SERPINA5
) influenced COVID-19 pathogenesis via the extrinsic CCC pathway. Upregulated
FGG
and
FGB
likely promoted fibrotic lung damage and inflammatory activation of the extrinsic coagulation pathway, while reduced
F2
and
SERPINA5
levels may enhance SARS-CoV-2 infection and impair antiviral responses.
We further analyzed the druggability of the four hub genes (
FGG
,
FGB
,
F2
, and
SERPINA5
). According to the OpenTargets database, only
SERPINA5
is not currently a target of any known FDA-approved drug. Despite this, numerous studies report decreased
SERPINA5
expression in multiple cancers, including hepatocellular carcinoma [
43
], ovarian cancer [
44
], and breast cancer [
45
]. Furthermore, low
SERPINA5
expression is associated with worse survival in breast cancer [
45
]. Therefore, although no known drug targeting
SERPINA5
was identified in the OpenTargets database, these findings support its potential as a cancer biomarker.
This study has several limitations. First, proteomic data were compiled from multiple studies utilizing diverse samples and methodologies, potentially introducing heterogeneity. Second, the patient cohorts varied in disease severity, vaccination status, comorbidities, and infecting SARS-CoV-2 variants; we did not analyze the potential influence of these factors. Third, while we performed meta-analysis on hub genes identified in two or more independent studies, only two genes (
FGB
and
SERPINA5
) were ultimately verified. Finally, the specific functions of
FGB
and
SERPINA5
in COVID-19 patients were not experimentally investigated.
Conclusion
Our bioinformatic analysis of CCC pathway proteins discovered 58 DEPs mapping to 88 genes. Four hub genes (
FGB
,
FGG
,
F2
, and
SERPINA5
) exhibited recurrent dysregulation in COVID-19 vs. healthy controls across ≥ 2 studies.
FGB
and
SERPINA5
were validated via meta-analysis and immunohistochemistry as potential diagnostic biomarkers/therapeutic targets. Findings confirm prior proteomic reports, advancing understanding of COVID-19 pathogenesis and identifying biomarkers for diagnosis and treatment.
